public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 229

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/229](https://www.erdosproblems.com/229)
- [BaSc72] Barth, K. F. and Schneider, W. J., On a problem of Erd\H{o}s concerning the zeros of the
  derivatives of an entire function. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1972), 229--232.
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos229

/--
Let $(S_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of sets of complex numbers, none of which have a finite
limit point. Does there exist an entire transcendental function $f(z)$ such that, for all $n \ge 1$, there
exists some $k_n \ge 0$ such that $f^{(k_n)}(z) = 0$ for all $z \in S_n$.

This is Problem 2.30 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

Solved in the affirmative by Barth and Schneider [BaSc72].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 30, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos229.lean"]
theorem erdos_229 :
    letI := Polynomial.algebraPi ℂ ℂ ℂ
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ (S : ℕ → Set ℂ), (∀ n, derivedSet (S n) = ∅) →
    ∃ (f : ℂ → ℂ), Transcendental (Polynomial ℂ) f ∧ Differentiable ℂ f ∧ ∀ n ≥ 1,
      ∃ k, ∀ z ∈ S n, iteratedDeriv k f z = 0 := by
  sorry

/--
Let $\{S_k\}$ be any sequence of sets in the complex plane, each of which has no finite
limit point. Then there exists a sequence $\{n_k\}$ of positive integers and a
transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that $f^{(n_k)}(z) = 0$ if $z \in S_k$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 30]
theorem theorem_1
    {S : ℕ → Set ℂ}
    (h : ∀ (k), derivedSet (S k) = ∅) :
  letI := Polynomial.algebraPi ℂ ℂ ℂ
  ∃ (f : ℂ → ℂ) (n : ℕ → ℕ),
    Differentiable ℂ f ∧ Transcendental (Polynomial ℂ) f ∧ ∀ k, 0 < n k ∧ ∀ {z} (_: z ∈ S k),
      iteratedDeriv (n k) f z = 0 := by
  sorry

end Erdos229

findings.description: The docstring identifies this as “Problem 2.30 in [Ha74],” but [Ha74] is specifically the 1974 “New problems” chapter, pp. 155–180. Problem 2.30 belongs to Hayman’s 1967 problem collection; the 1974 new-problems chapter introduces entire-function Problems 2.33–2.46. This is a misplaced reference, not a mathematical error in the theorem.
findings.source_evidence: Hayman–Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory, arXiv:1809.07200v2, states Problem 2.30 and its Barth–Schneider update. Tables 1–2 identify source A as Hayman’s 1967 book and assign Problems 2.1–2.32 to A, while assigning 2.33–2.46 to the 1974 source B. Cambridge’s chapter records distinguish “Progress on the previous problems,” pp. 143–154 (doi:10.1017/CBO9780511662263.033), from “New problems,” pp. 155–180 (doi:10.1017/CBO9780511662263.034).
findings.suggested_fix: Cite Hayman, Research Problems in Function Theory, Athlone Press, 1967, Problem 2.30, or Hayman–Lingham’s updated edition, Problem 2.30. If retaining the 1974 reference for the progress update, cite “Progress on the previous problems,” pp. 143–154, rather than “New problems.”

reformulations.difference: The source asks for a transcendental entire function, conventionally an entire function that is not a polynomial. Lean instead requires algebraic transcendence over Polynomial ℂ, using Polynomial.algebraPi.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Polynomial.algebraPi sends a polynomial p to the function z ↦ p.eval z. Thus algebraicity means satisfying a nonzero polynomial equation P(z,f(z)) = 0. An entire algebraic function is a polynomial: polynomial root bounds give polynomial growth, and Cauchy estimates force its Taylor series to terminate. Conversely, a polynomial function p(z) satisfies Y − p(X) = 0. Therefore, under Differentiable ℂ f, the Lean transcendence condition is exactly non-polynomiality. The equivalence and its lift to the complete quantified statement were proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean without sorry dependencies.

reformulations.difference: As in the main theorem, analytic transcendence is expressed as Transcendental (Polynomial ℂ) f rather than explicitly saying that f is not a polynomial.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For entire functions, algebraicity over ℂ[X] under the evaluation algebra structure is equivalent to being a polynomial function. Consequently its negation agrees with the source’s “transcendental entire.” The equivalence was proved and lifted to this theorem’s existential function-and-order-sequence statement in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean; the resulting proof depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

Hayman, W. K. and Lingham, E. F., Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition), arXiv:1809.07200v2: LaTeX source https://arxiv.org/e-print/1809.07200v2, especially Problem 2.30, Update 2.30, and Tables 1–3.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalization was found in either declaration. The affirmative answer, solved categories, and external formal-proof record agree with the accessible sources. Scratch checks verified empty and singleton sets, exclusion of polynomial functions, derivative orders 0 and 1, differentiability of all iterated derivatives, equivalence of the derived-set hypothesis with finite intersection with every compact set, and harmless sequence reindexing. Direct erdosproblems.com access returned Cloudflare challenges, and full publisher PDFs were unavailable; comparison instead used the primary-paper abstract, Hayman–Lingham’s statement and update, Cambridge’s bibliographic material, and the current mathematical-data mirror. All experiments were confined to /workspace/review/.
